item.title: US futures look to rebound after tech rout but the real test is still ahead
item.description:
US futures are faring better to start the new week, taking some relief after the beating suffered last week. Tech stocks in particular were battered hard, with the Nasdaq snapping a four-week winning streak to end the week down by over 4%. The S&P 500 also fell by roughly 2%, its worst weekly showing since June.

But so far today, things are looking up again. Nasdaq futures are up 1.4% while S&P 500 futures are up 0.8% on the day. So, what's changed over the weekend?

For one, the bond market seems to be offering up more breathing room for broader markets. 10-year Treasury yields are down slightly to 5.06% now, helped by softer oil prices amid prospects of easing Russian sanctions. So, that is taking some pressure off richly valued tech stocks, whose appeal is particularly sensitive to borrowing costs.

Having said that, I still wouldn't take this as an all-clear signal just yet.

It was rather evident that the selloff on Wall Street last week wasn't just about the bond market. Despite hotter-than-expected inflation data, Treasury yields fell and yet tech stocks suffered all through the week. Is it a case of investors waking up to the struggles in market breadth and momentum? Or perhaps the case that investors are questioning further the enormous sums being poured into AI infrastructure, especially with financing costs remaining elevated?

Either way, the latter will be one to be mindful about as we get into trading this week.

Netflix, Meta, and Tesla will all feature on the earnings calendar in the week ahead. And in particular, I would single out Meta's results as being rather crucial as investors will look to scrutinise the firm's AI spending plans and profit margins.

Besides that, we'll also get earnings from IBM and Lam Research with the latter perhaps offering clues on whether underlying chip demand remains resilient.

Beyond earnings, Friday's US flash PMI readings and the direction of Treasury yields will also be worth watching. For now though, lower yields might be giving tech stocks an excuse to bounce. But looking to the days ahead, I would argue that this week's earnings will need to give investors a reason to keep buying.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive Asia-Pacific market news: China beats, the euro wobbles and oil dips
item.description:
Summary:

  • The euro opened lower on escalating riots in France, drone incidents over the Black Sea and US warnings over EU tech rules, then recovered most of the gap
  • Oil edged lower after Trump signed an order waiving some sanctions and duties on Russian energy, with the US set to receive more than 300,000 tonnes of Russian diesel
  • Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and Iran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz limited oil’s downside
  • Putin has proposed a three-way meeting with Trump and Xi on Ukraine, possibly at next month’s APEC summit
  • China’s Q3 GDP grew 4.5% y/y, beating forecasts, with September retail sales and industrial output firmer, though investment stayed weak
  • RBA Assistant Governor Kent said neutral rates appear to be rising and questioned whether policy is restrictive enough
  • BOJ Governor Ueda said anchoring underlying inflation is becoming more important and that appropriate rate hikes help stabilise JGBs
  • Gold edged higher, AI data centre financing came under scrutiny, and crypto network Qubic halted after a wallet theft

The euro opened the week lower as escalating riots in France added to a run of risk headlines in Europe. Romania’s defence ministry said its F-16s shot down two drones over Romanian territorial waters in the Black Sea on Saturday, while the US ambassador to the European Union warned that European companies could face severe retaliation in the US market if Brussels reserves satellite-to-phone spectrum for local operators, a move that would limit SpaceX. The ambassador also criticised EU cloud rules and fines under the Digital Markets Act. The single currency has since recovered most of its opening gap.

Oil prices dipped after President Donald Trump signed an executive order waiving certain sanctions, restrictions and duties on Russian energy. The US is expected to initially receive more than 300,000 tonnes of Russian diesel. Losses did not extend, given  reports of further Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, while Iran reiterated that its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz depends on Washington meeting its demands.

On diplomacy, Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a three-way meeting with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month to discuss ending the war in Ukraine, a format that would exclude Kyiv, the Wall Street Journal reported. The Kremlin confirmed talks on a possible meeting but said there is no agreement on whether it will go ahead or what it would cover, and a senior US official said Trump has not agreed to a summit.

Gold edged higher, with softer oil prices offering some support.

China provided the main data of the day. Third-quarter GDP grew 4.5% from a year earlier, ahead of the 4.4% forecast and up from 4.3% in the second quarter, which had been the slowest pace in more than three years. Quarterly growth was 1.2%, beating expectations of 1.1%. Growth for the first nine months was 4.6%, within the government’s 4.5% to 5.0% target, which may ease pressure for more aggressive stimulus. September data was also firmer: industrial output rose 5.5%, its fastest in six months, helped by exports of AI-related technology goods, while retail sales grew 1.1%, up from 0.4% in August and the quickest since March. Investment remained the weak spot, with fixed asset investment down 7.2% over the first nine months and property investment down around 20.5%.

In central bank commentary, Reserve Bank of Australia Assistant Governor Christopher Kent said there is reasonable evidence that neutral interest rates are rising in Australia and abroad. He said he is confident policy is somewhat restrictive but questioned whether it is restrictive enough. Kent noted household demand is softening, business credit remains strong and housing tax changes have supported monetary policy. He was cautious about reading too much into monthly jobs data but said the labour market has become less tight.

Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said anchoring underlying inflation around 2% is becoming more important, pointing to supply-driven price pressures from Middle East energy costs and demand-driven inflation from strong AI-related demand. He said the bank’s bond taper plan is unchanged and declined to pre-set conditions for action in the JGB market, citing rapid yield rises or disruption to market functioning as possible factors. Ueda added that appropriate rate hikes help stabilise government bonds. The yen edged higher but gave up its modest gains as the session progressed.

Elsewhere, scrutiny of the US AI infrastructure build-out intensified after reports that at least 47 large data centre projects have been delayed, withdrawn or blocked this year, as debt tied to AI infrastructure groups sold off. In crypto, layer 1 network Qubic halted its blockchain after an attacker exploited weak randomness in wallet seed generation to drain around 2.94 trillion QU, roughly $1.3 million, from 1,404 wallets. About 87% of the stolen funds remain frozen on the network, and its validators will decide on recovery.

Looking ahead, markets will watch whether the euro’s recovery holds as French unrest develops, how oil balances easier Russian supply against Middle East risks, and whether firmer Chinese data and hawkish-leaning central bank commentary reshape rate expectations.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Crypto: Qubic halts network after weak wallet seeds let attacker drain 1,404 wallets
item.description:
The direct market fallout is contained: QUBIC is a small-cap token, the loss is modest in dollar terms, and the selling has so far stayed confined to the token itself rather than spreading to the wider crypto market. The bigger near-term pressure is liquidity, with the network halted and exchanges suspending deposits and withdrawals, leaving holders unable to move tokens until the chain restarts. How the Computor vote handles restitution is likely to matter more for the token’s recovery than the theft itself, since a clean, transparent outcome could steady confidence while a drawn-out freeze would add to doubts. The episode may also renew scrutiny of other wallet providers’ key-generation practices.

--- Qubic’s blockchain held up but its wallet keys did not, and while freezing the network saved most of the stolen tokens, it also shows how much power a small validator group holds over users’ funds.

Summary:

  • An attacker drained 1,404 Qubic wallets of around 2.94 trillion QU, roughly $1.3 million, in under two hours on October 17-18 UTC
  • The flaw was weak randomness in wallet seed generation, not the Qubic protocol, and is fixed in version 4.26.4
  • Wallets created via browsers on iPhone and iPad, Safari on Mac, and older iOS app versions were exposed
  • The network halted at tick 85,371,949, with around 87% of stolen funds frozen on-chain and the rest frozen at MEXC
  • Exchanges suspended QUBIC deposits and withdrawals, and the token fell more than 10%
  • Qubic’s Computor validators will decide on recovery and any restitution

Layer 1 blockchain Qubic has halted its network after an attacker exploited weak randomness in wallet seed generation to drain 1,404 wallets of around 2.94 trillion QU tokens, worth roughly $1.3 million, over a window of less than two hours late on October 17 and early October 18 UTC, according to a post from the project.

Qubic stressed that the flaw sat in the tool used to create wallet seeds rather than in the blockchain protocol itself. The affected code relied on a random number function that is not designed for cryptographic secrets, which meant seeds that looked long and secure were in practice predictable enough for an attacker to reconstruct a smaller pool of likely candidates and scan them for funded wallets. Wallets created through browsers on iPhone and iPad, through Safari on Mac until October 18, and through older versions of the Qubic iOS app were exposed. The project says the issue is fixed in version 4.26.4.

Validators stopped the network at tick 85,371,949. Around 87% of the stolen tokens remain on Qubic and are frozen by the halt, while the remaining 13% or so was sent to the MEXC exchange, which froze the receiving account. Other exchanges have suspended QUBIC deposits and withdrawals. The token fell more than 10% after the attack, and the project carries a market value of only around $60 million, which keeps the incident small in dollar terms.

---

Key terms explained

Wallet seed A string of characters, often shown as a list of words, that generates and restores a crypto wallet’s private keys. Anyone who has the seed controls the funds, so it must be impossible to guess.

Randomness in seed generation Seeds need to come from a truly unpredictable source. Some ordinary programming functions only look random and follow patterns, which can let an attacker narrow down the possible seeds and find funded wallets. That’s what happened at Qubic.

Layer 1 blockchain A base blockchain network with its own rules and token, such as Bitcoin or Ethereum, as opposed to an app or network built on top of another chain.

Computors Qubic’s equivalent of validators: a fixed group of operators who process transactions and vote on network decisions, including whether to halt the chain and what happens to frozen funds.

Tick Qubic’s unit of network time, similar to a block number on other chains. Halting at a specific tick marks the exact point after which no transactions were processed.

---

The episode offers two lessons for crypto users. The first is that a secure blockchain does not guarantee secure funds: control rests on private keys, and keys are only as strong as the software that generates them. Similar weak-randomness flaws have hit other wallet tools in recent years. The second is that a network able to pause itself and freeze balances is making a trade-off. The halt protected most of the stolen funds, but it also shows that a relatively small group of validators, known on Qubic as Computors, can stop transactions and decide what happens to user assets.

That group now holds the key decision. Readers should watch when and how the network restarts, whether the Computor vote delivers restitution for victims, whether MEXC returns the frozen portion, and what the promised technical report reveals. A clean recovery would support confidence in Qubic’s governance, while a prolonged halt or a contested vote would raise harder questions about how decentralised the network really is. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China Q3 GDP beats forecasts at 4.5%, retail sales grow at fastest pace since March
item.description:
A modest beat across the board supports the Australian and New Zealand dollars and broader Asian risk sentiment, though the relief is tempered by weak investment. For oil, firmer industrial output and retail sales from the world’s largest crude importer offer some support to the demand side, at a time when Iran war disruptions are already keeping supply risk elevated. Industrial metals and iron ore face a mixed message: stronger factory activity helps, but a 20.6% drop in property investment is a clear drag on construction demand. Reduced odds of aggressive stimulus may cap enthusiasm for Chinese equities, which are already leaning on state support, and lower expectations for a cut at Tuesday’s LPR decision.

China’s economy has climbed back into Beijing’s target range on the strength of its factories and exporters, giving policymakers room to keep holding back the big stimulus that weak consumers and a broken property market still need.

Summary:

  • GDP (Q3, Y/Y): 4.5%, expected 4.4%, prior 4.3%
  • GDP (Q3, Q/Q): 1.2%, expected 1.1%, prior 0.9%
  • Retail sales (Sep, Y/Y): 1.1%, expected 0.5%, prior 0.4%
  • Industrial production (Sep, Y/Y): 5.5%, expected 5.4%, prior 5.2%
  • Fixed asset investment (YTD, Y/Y): -7.2%, expected -7.3%, prior -7.2%
  • Growth for the first nine months was 4.6%; property investment fell 20.6% and infrastructure investment fell 4.2%
  • The beat eases pressure for large-scale stimulus; the LPR decision is due Tuesday

China’s economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, with GDP rising 4.5% from a year earlier, landing at the bottom of Beijing’s annual target range and easing pressure on policymakers to roll out more aggressive stimulus.

The figure, released by the National Bureau of Statistics on Monday, beat the 4.4% forecast in a Reuters poll and picked up from 4.3% in the second quarter, which had been the weakest pace in more than three years. On a quarterly basis, the economy expanded 1.2%, ahead of expectations for 1.1% and up from 0.9%. Growth for the first nine months of the year was 4.6%, within the government’s 4.5% to 5.0% target.

The September activity data also came in slightly firmer than expected. Industrial output grew 5.5% from a year earlier, its fastest pace in six months and up from 5.2% in August, supported by strong exports of AI-related technology goods. Retail sales rose 1.1%, more than double August’s 0.4% and the quickest growth since March, beating forecasts.

Investment remained the weak spot. Fixed asset investment fell 7.2% in the first nine months, unchanged from the January to August period and marginally better than the expected 7.3% decline. Property investment slumped 20.6% over the same period, and infrastructure investment shrank 4.2% despite a series of measures aimed at reviving it.

Beijing has recently expanded support for home buyers, steered cheaper credit toward infrastructure and technology, allocated 550 billion yuan of unused government debt quotas to ease local government finances, broadened loan interest subsidies for small private firms and consumers, and tapped an 800 billion yuan policy financing tool for infrastructure. Earlier on Monday, data showed new home prices falling at a slightly slower pace in September, though still declining.

The results reinforce the picture of a two-speed economy, in which factory output and exports driven by the global technology boom offset weak consumption, private investment and property. That reliance on exports carries its own risks. China’s trade surplus widened more than expected in September and is on track to exceed last year’s record of $1.2 trillion, adding to frictions with partners including the European Union, which has agreed a deal with Beijing to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle shipments.

With growth back within the target range, the case for large-scale stimulus has weakened, and policymakers appear content to rely on targeted support. Tuesday’s loan prime rate decision will be the next signal of Beijing’s policy stance.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China moves to prop up stocks with selling curbs, buybacks after 10% slide this year
item.description:
State buying and selling curbs typically put a floor under Chinese equities in the short term, so near-term downside in mainland indices may be more limited than global tech peers suggest. That support is administrative rather than fundamental, and rallies built on directed buying have often faded once the intervention eases. The yuan and Chinese government bonds, which have held up well this year, are unlikely to be driven by the measures. Monday’s GDP and activity data matter more: a weak print could raise hopes of fiscal stimulus, which would give equities firmer footing than market support alone. Broader Asian tech sentiment will hinge on global AI valuations.

  • China Q3 GDP beats estimates, as does September retail sales

Beijing is reaching for its familiar toolkit of state buying and polite instructions not to sell, but propping up share prices is easier than fixing the weak demand dragging on the economy.

Summary:

  • Chinese regulators asked companies and state-backed funds to buy shares and guided some investors to sell less, Bloomberg reported
  • Major insurers were told to report equity holdings, avoid crystallising losses below cost and align investments with economic goals
  • The “national team” of state funds was asked to speed up purchases, with signs of heavy ETF inflows
  • The benchmark index is down about 10% this year and hit its lowest since August 2025, amid a global sell-off in AI-linked tech
  • Chinese bonds and the yuan have held up, with the yuan up more than 4% against the dollar this year
  • The measures come ahead of Q3 GDP, expected to show growth below Beijing’s target

Chinese authorities have stepped in to support the country’s stock market, asking state funds and companies to buy shares while discouraging some investors from selling, according to a Bloomberg report, as a tech-led slide pushed the benchmark index down about 10% this year.

Financial regulators held a meeting on Thursday at which they asked companies and state-backed funds to purchase stocks and guided some investors to reduce selling, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter. State funds, often referred to as the “national team”, were asked to accelerate their buying, and separate reporting pointed to heavy inflows into exchange-traded funds consistent with state purchases.

Major insurers received informal window guidance to report their equity holdings, avoid locking in losses on positions trading below cost, and align their investment decisions with broader economic objectives. Regulators did not respond to requests for comment.

The steps build on commitments from the securities regulator earlier this month to strengthen market-stabilisation mechanisms, widen channels for long-term institutional money, encourage higher dividends and share buybacks, and prepare further policy tools.

The intervention follows a sharp sell-off concentrated in technology and AI-related shares, which had led earlier gains. The benchmark index closed on Thursday at its lowest since August 2025, while the tech-heavy ChiNext index fell almost 3% that day. The weakness was part of a wider global retreat from AI-linked stocks, with South Korea’s Kospi falling more than 7% and Japan’s Nikkei 225 almost 5% on the same day as investors reassessed valuations and interest-rate expectations.

According to Bloomberg, authorities are concerned about market fragility and want to prevent selling pressure from feeding a downward spiral.

Notably, the stress has been concentrated in equities rather than spreading across Chinese assets. Government bonds have rallied this year, pushing the 10-year yield close to its lowest in more than a year, while the yuan has gained more than 4% against the dollar, outperforming its Asian peers.

The support measures come as the economy struggles with weak consumer demand, sluggish private investment and a prolonged property downturn. Monday’s third-quarter GDP data is expected to show growth below Beijing’s 4.5% to 5.0% target.

That sets up a broader test. Administrative steps such as selling curbs and directed buying can steady prices in the short term, but they do little to address the weak domestic demand behind the economic slowdown. Whether Beijing follows up with more substantial fiscal or monetary support may matter more for a durable recovery in Chinese stocks. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China home price declines ease in September, ahead of Q3 GDP seen at 4.4%
item.description:
Smaller price declines are mildly encouraging for Chinese property developers and for sentiment toward the yuan, but they are unlikely to shift the market narrative on their own. Oil is the bigger channel: as the largest crude importer, China’s domestic demand matters for prices at a time when the Iran war is already squeezing Gulf supply, and any weak consumption or investment data would temper the demand side. The Australian and New Zealand dollars, as China proxies, are exposed to a disappointment in the GDP and activity figures. Iron ore and industrial metals will take their cue from the property investment number in particular.

  • PBOC sets USD/ CNY reference rate for today at 6.7208 (vs. estimate at 6.6897)

China’s home prices are still falling, just a little more slowly, which is about as much good news as the property sector has offered in a while, and the main data due shortly is unlikely to change that story.

Summary:

  • New home prices (M/M, Sep): -0.14% (prior -0.17%)
  • New home prices (Y/Y, Sep): -2.8% (prior -3.0%)
  • Used home prices (M/M, Sep): -0.26% (prior -0.31%)
  • Prices are still falling across measures, but the pace of decline eased; late-September support measures have yet to fully feed through
  • Q3 GDP is due at 02:00 GMT (22:00 US Eastern Sunday) and is forecast at 4.4% y/y and 1.1% q/q, against a 4.5% to 5.0% target
  • September forecasts: industrial production about 5.3% to 5.5%, retail sales under 1%, fixed asset investment about -7.5% YTD; LPR decision due Tuesday

China’s new home prices fell again in September, but at a slightly slower pace than in August, offering a tentative sign that the property slump may be losing some momentum ahead of the release of third-quarter GDP and a batch of activity data at 02:00 GMT (22:00 US Eastern on Sunday).

New home prices declined 0.14% from the previous month, compared with a 0.17% drop in August. From a year earlier, prices were down 2.8%, a smaller fall than August’s 3.0%. Prices of existing homes fell 0.26% on the month, after a 0.31% decline previously.

The figures still show prices falling on every measure, so any improvement is a matter of degree rather than a turn. Even so, the narrowing in both new and used home price declines comes after Beijing added targeted support for the sector in late September, including mortgage subsidies for some home purchases. Much of that support arrived too late to have a meaningful effect on September transactions, so October and November data will give a clearer read on whether it is gaining traction.

Property remains the biggest drag on China’s domestic economy, weighing on household wealth, consumer confidence and investment. That makes the housing figures an important backdrop for the main data due shortly.

Economists polled by Reuters and AFP expect third-quarter growth of 4.4% from a year earlier, up slightly from 4.3% in the second quarter but below Beijing’s 4.5% to 5.0% target for 2026. Quarterly growth is forecast at 1.1%, from 0.9%.

The September activity figures are expected to show a familiar split. Industrial production is forecast to grow around 5.3% to 5.5% from a year earlier, from 5.2% in August, supported by strong exports of AI-related hardware. Retail sales are expected to grow by less than 1%, little better than August’s 0.4%. Fixed asset investment is forecast to contract by around 7.5% in the year to date, with some forecasts pointing to property investment falling by as much as 27% from a year earlier.

Higher energy costs linked to the US war with Iran add a further headwind for the world’s largest crude importer.

Weak domestic readings would add pressure on Beijing to speed up stimulus, with Tuesday’s loan prime rate decision the next policy marker. Goldman Sachs has warned that a second straight quarter of growth below 4.5% would increase pressure on policymakers.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman Sachs sees S&P 500 earnings at $415 in 2027 but warns narrow leadership is a risk
item.description:
Goldman’s view supports staying invested in US equities, but it points to rotation rather than broad gains. The recent slide in the momentum factor suggests that rotation may already be under way, with crowded AI and mega-cap trades most exposed. Oil is a key swing factor: elevated crude prices tied to the Iran war are part of what restrains growth in Goldman’s base case, so any further energy shock would delay the consumer recovery it is banking on for 2027. Rate-sensitive and lower-income consumer names stand to benefit most if inflation and yields ease. Third-quarter earnings over the coming weeks will test whether profit forecasts hold up.

---

Earlier:

  • Only a third of the US data centre pipeline looks credible as AI financing strains build

---

Goldman still sees room for US stocks to climb, but with the index propped up by a narrow group of winners, it is telling investors to look for the next leaders rather than chase the last ones.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs strategists led by Ben Snider expect US stocks to keep rising on earnings growth, with slower growth tempering rather than ending the rally
  • The S&P 500 was about 2% below its record, while the median stock was around 15% below its high; market breadth is near its narrowest since the dot-com era
  • Goldman’s momentum factor fell 8% in one week, highlighting the risk to crowded trades
  • Goldman forecasts S&P 500 EPS of $375 in 2026 and $415 in 2027, with its 2028 estimate about 7% below consensus
  • AI capex accounts for about half of S&P 500 earnings growth, a boost expected to fade
  • Goldman favours lagging consumer stocks, particularly those tied to lower-income households and experiences, on expected real income gains in 2027

Goldman Sachs expects the US stock market rally to continue on the back of rising corporate profits, but its equity strategists warn that unusually narrow market leadership leaves investors who chase recent winners exposed to a sharp reversal.

In a report dated 16 October, a team led by strategist Ben Snider argued that slowing economic and earnings growth should moderate equity returns rather than bring the advance to an end. Their preferred opportunity lies in consumer stocks that have lagged the market, which they expect to benefit from improving household purchasing power next year.

The concern sits beneath the headline index. When the report was written, the S&P 500 was only about 2% below its record high, yet the typical stock in the index was around 15% below its own peak. Goldman’s measure of market breadth was close to its narrowest since the dot-com era. That gap is a risk for momentum strategies, which favour recent outperformers: either lagging stocks catch up, or the leaders fall back toward the pack, and both outcomes would hurt trades built on the previous leadership. Goldman’s momentum factor dropped 8% in a single week, showing how quickly those positions can unwind.

Earnings remain the main support. Goldman forecasts S&P 500 earnings per share of $375 in 2026 and $415 in 2027. Stripping out one-off accounting effects, it puts underlying growth at around 29% this year and 18% next. But the bank sees less room for the large upward revisions that have powered stocks, and its 2028 estimate of $460 a share sits roughly 7% below consensus.

Artificial intelligence is central to that outlook. Goldman estimates AI capital spending accounts for about half of S&P 500 earnings growth, a contribution it expects to fade as spending growth slows and depreciation costs rise. That view sits alongside other recent signals on the AI buildout, from forecasts showing memory costs swallowing a growing share of hyperscaler budgets to reports of data centre projects stalling on grid power constraints.

Higher interest rates and oil prices are also expected to weigh on activity. Goldman’s consumer thesis rests on those pressures easing in 2027, with lower inflation, energy prices and rates lifting real incomes, particularly for lower-income households. It forecasts real income growth for the bottom fifth of earners accelerating from 0.4% in 2026 to 1.8% in 2027. Hedge fund exposure to consumer discretionary stocks is near multiyear lows, which could amplify any recovery, though Goldman is selective, favouring lower-income consumer names and experience-related businesses rather than the sector as a whole.

Historically, periods of positive but slowing growth have still delivered gains, driven by earnings rather than rising valuations, and have favoured companies with durable growth and lower volatility. The risk is a deeper slowdown. With cyclical stocks already losing ground to defensives, the path for the market’s recent leaders looks harder from here.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: More BoJ’s Ueda names two factors for bond market action, keeps JGB taper plan unchanged
item.description:
The yen’s muted response suggests markets saw little new here beyond confirmation of the BoJ’s existing approach. For Japanese government bonds, Ueda’s message cuts two ways: he is not offering a backstop at any particular yield level, yet he is signalling the bank will act if the selloff becomes disorderly. Super-long JGBs, the most sensitive part of the curve, are where any test of that commitment would show up first. His argument that falling behind on rates would push yields higher strengthens the hawkish framing ahead of 30 October. Global bond investors will watch closely, given Japan’s role in global yields and capital flows.

-

Ueda is telling bond markets that the best protection against a disorderly selloff is a BoJ that keeps raising rates on time, not a promise to step in at a set level.

Summary:

  • BoJ Governor Kazuo Ueda said there is no change to the bank’s basic stance on tapering its bond purchases
  • He said it would be inappropriate to say in advance when the BoJ might conduct emergency bond market operations
  • Any decision would weigh market conditions comprehensively, such as a rapid rise in long-term rates or signs of destabilising market function
  • He expects long-term rates to rise steadily in line with any increases in the policy rate
  • He warned that failing to adjust rates appropriately could push long-term yields higher on inflation overshoot fears
  • He said financial conditions remain accommodative; the yen barely moved

Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said the central bank’s basic approach to reducing its bond purchases is unchanged, and declined to say in advance when it might step into the government bond market with emergency operations.

Speaking in the same appearance in which he stressed the importance of anchoring underlying inflation around 2%, Ueda said the BoJ would look comprehensively at market conditions before deciding whether to intervene. He pointed to two considerations in particular: whether long-term interest rates are rising at a rapid pace, and whether bond market functioning is showing signs of instability.

Ueda also set out how he expects short and long-term rates to interact as policy tightens. If the BoJ raises its short-term policy rate, he said, long-term rates are likely to rise steadily in line with those steps. But if the policy rate is not adjusted appropriately, he warned, market concerns about the risk of inflation overshooting could push long-term yields higher.

In effect, Ueda argued that well-calibrated rate increases are a stabilising force for the Japanese government bond market rather than a threat to it. By conducting policy appropriately to achieve its 2% inflation goal, he said, the BoJ can help stabilise JGBs. He added that financial conditions remain accommodative, a reminder that policy is still supportive of growth even after the bank’s recent hikes.

The remarks address a tension that has run through the BoJ’s exit from years of ultra-loose policy. The bank has been gradually scaling back its bond buying while raising rates, leaving investors alert to the risk of disorderly moves in long-term yields. By declining to set a trigger for emergency buying, Ueda keeps the bank’s options open while signalling that intervention would be reserved for genuinely disorderly conditions rather than a steady repricing.

The comments also reinforce the hawkish tone of his earlier remarks, framing further rate increases as consistent with market stability. The BoJ’s policy rate stands at 1.25%, with the next decision due on 30 October.

The yen was little changed as Ueda spoke, suggesting the bond market comments largely confirmed existing expectations.

item.title: BoJ’s Ueda says anchoring inflation at 2% more important as AI demand, energy lift prices
item.description:
The yen’s gain was modest, suggesting markets read the remarks as reinforcing the BoJ’s existing tightening bias rather than signalling an October move. Oil is a central channel for Japan: as a heavy energy importer, it feels Middle East price spikes directly, and higher crude both lifts inflation and widens the trade bill. That cuts both ways for the yen. By framing AI demand and the labour market as genuine demand pressures, Ueda gives hawks a stronger footing, which could support Japanese government bond yields at the short end. The October meeting’s assessment of underlying inflation is now the main catalyst for the yen.

---

Ueda is quietly making the case that Japan’s inflation is no longer just an imported energy story, and that shift is what would ultimately justify the BoJ’s next hike.

Summary:

  • BoJ Governor Kazuo Ueda said anchoring underlying inflation around 2% is becoming more important
  • He said Japan is seeing a positive cycle of rising wages and recovering prices
  • He attributed supply-driven inflation to Middle East energy costs, and demand-driven inflation to strong global AI demand boosting capex, exports and goods prices
  • A moderate recovery and tight labour market are also pushing inflation higher
  • The yen edged slightly higher after the remarks
  • The BoJ’s policy rate is 1.25%, with the next decision due 30 October

Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said it is becoming more important to anchor underlying inflation around the central bank’s 2% target, setting out a case in which both supply shocks and strong demand are now pushing prices higher in Japan.

In remarks reported early on Monday, Asian time, Ueda said Japan is seeing a positive cycle in which wages are rising and prices are recovering. He then distinguished between two sources of price pressure. On the supply side, he said the conflict in the Middle East is lifting energy costs and a range of other prices. On the demand side, he said very strong global demand linked to artificial intelligence is boosting domestic capital spending, exports and the prices of various goods.

Ueda added that Japan’s moderate economic recovery and a tight labour market are also adding to inflation.

The distinction matters for policy. Central banks typically look through supply-driven inflation, such as an energy price spike, on the basis that it should fade. Demand-driven inflation, by contrast, is the kind monetary policy is designed to address. By highlighting AI-related demand and a tight jobs market alongside the energy shock, Ueda appears to be building the argument that recent price gains are not purely temporary.

The comments build on remarks late last week, when Ueda said the BoJ would continue to raise interest rates as underlying inflation approaches 2%, and that the timing and pace of increases would depend on exchange rates, AI-driven demand and developments in the Middle East. He also said policymakers would discuss at their next meeting whether to revise their assessment of underlying inflation.

The BoJ’s short-term policy rate stands at 1.25%, and the bank’s next decision is due on 30 October. Market pricing has leaned against a move at that meeting, but language stressing the need to anchor inflation keeps the prospect of a hike in the near future firmly in view.

The yen edged slightly higher after the comments.

The key question for markets is whether the BoJ formally upgrades its view of underlying inflation at the October meeting. Such a shift would signal that the conditions for the next rate rise are falling into place, even if the bank chooses to wait.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: RBA’s Kent says neutral rate is rising, questions if policy is restrictive enough
item.description:
Kent’s remarks pull in two directions, which may limit any lasting move in the Australian dollar. Endorsing the post-jobs repricing suggests the RBA is comfortable with markets scaling back near-term hike bets, a mild negative for the currency and supportive for short-end bonds. But the neutral rate argument is a hawkish undercurrent, since it implies the 4.60% cash rate may be doing less work than assumed. That makes the 28 October inflation data the pivotal event: a hot print would revive November hike pricing quickly, while a soft one would likely cement a pause. Rate-sensitive sectors, especially property and banks, will be tracking that shift closely.

---

Earlier:

  • Euro slides against Australian dollar as three European headwinds hit early trade

---Kent is happy for markets to pare November hike bets after a weak jobs report, but his warning that neutral rates are rising leaves the RBA plenty of room to tighten again if inflation runs hot.

Summary:

  • RBA Assistant Governor (Financial Markets) Christopher Kent said there is reasonable evidence neutral rates are rising in Australia and abroad
  • He is confident policy is somewhat restrictive but questioned whether it is restrictive enough
  • Household demand is softening, business credit remains strong, and housing tax changes have helped monetary policy
  • Kent is cautious on monthly jobs data but said the labour market has become less tight
  • He said the market move after last week’s weak jobs report, a lower Australian dollar, lower short-term rates and reduced near-term hike odds, made sense
  • The cash rate is 4.60% after four hikes this year; Q3 CPI is due 28 October, ahead of the 2 to 3 November RBA meeting

Reserve Bank of Australia Assistant Governor Christopher Kent said there is reasonable evidence that neutral interest rates are rising, both in Australia and overseas, raising the question of whether monetary policy is as tight as it appears, even after four rate increases this year.

Speaking at a fireside chat at the Commonwealth Bank’s Global Markets Conference in Sydney, Kent, who oversees financial markets at the central bank, said he was confident policy is somewhat restrictive but questioned whether it is restrictive enough.

The neutral rate is the level of interest rates that neither stimulates nor restrains the economy. If it has drifted higher, a cash rate that looks tight on paper may be exerting less pressure on demand and inflation than policymakers had assumed, which would strengthen the case for keeping rates higher for longer or tightening further.

Kent’s remarks come as the RBA weighs its next move. The board lifted the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.60% on 29 September, its fourth increase of 2026, citing inflation that remains too high, energy prices pushed up by the broadening conflict in the Middle East, and lingering capacity pressures. It said further increases were possible if needed.

On the economy, Kent said household demand is softening, while business credit growth remains strong. He described recent tax changes affecting housing as helpful for monetary policy, a sign the bank sees fiscal settings working with it rather than against it on housing demand.

He was more cautious on the labour market. Kent said he was wary of reading too much into monthly employment figures, but acknowledged conditions have become less tight. Data last week showed employment fell by about 39,000 in September, against expectations of a gain of around 20,000, with the unemployment rate rising to 4.7%, the highest in around five years.

That report sent the Australian dollar and short-term interest rates lower as traders pared bets on a near-term hike. Kent said that market reaction made sense, a comment likely to be read as the bank seeing no reason to push back against the repricing.

Even so, the debate is far from settled. ANZ kept its call for a further 25 basis point increase in November after the jobs data, arguing that upward revisions to the bank’s inflation forecasts make a hike more likely than not.

The next key test is quarterly inflation data on 28 October, ahead of the RBA’s 2 to 3 November meeting. Kent’s comments on a rising neutral rate suggest that, if inflation surprises to the upside, the bank still sees room to tighten.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Microsoft quits Nscale UK data centre deal ahead of planned $3 billion IPO
item.description:
The report adds to pressure on AI infrastructure stocks already under strain, with CoreWeave’s sharp weekly fall showing investors are quicker to punish debt-funded buildouts. Nscale may face pressure to price its IPO more conservatively or delay it, and peers seeking capital could find the window narrower. For the energy complex, the story reinforces the view that grid capacity, not chips, is becoming the binding constraint on data centre growth. That supports utilities, independent power producers and gas-fired generation tied to data centre demand. For Microsoft itself, the move reads as capital discipline rather than a retreat from AI spending.

---

Earlier:

  • Only a third of the US data centre pipeline looks credible as AI financing strains build

---

Nscale has lost its anchor tenant in Essex not for lack of AI demand but for lack of electricity, a costly lesson to learn days before asking investors for $3 billion.

Summary:

  • Microsoft has pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale’s first British data centre, in Loughton, Essex, the Telegraph reported
  • No reason was given, but the site faces power connection delays reportedly stretching into the 2030s
  • Nscale says its relationship with Microsoft remains strong and is exploring other power sources and UK sites
  • Microsoft and Anthropic account for about 85% of Nscale’s contracts, according to its IPO filing
  • Nscale is seeking to raise up to $3 billion in an IPO, possibly as soon as October
  • Neocloud sentiment has soured, with CoreWeave down 25% last week and Australia’s Firmus scrapping its IPO

Microsoft has pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale’s first British data centre, according to a report in the Telegraph, dealing a blow to the AI infrastructure company as it prepares a listing that could raise up to $3 billion as soon as this month.

Microsoft had been expected to be the main customer at the planned site in Loughton, Essex. No reason for the withdrawal has been disclosed, and Microsoft did not comment on the report, which was picked up by Bloomberg on Sunday. The project has, however, been dogged by repeated delays, and local authorities have reportedly warned Nscale that it may not secure a grid power connection until the 2030s.

Nscale said its relationship with Microsoft remained strong and long term, and that the power constraints in Essex would not affect its other contracts. The company said it is exploring alternative power sources and additional UK locations.

The timing is awkward. Nscale’s IPO filing shows Microsoft and Anthropic together account for about 85% of its contracts, leaving the company heavily exposed to two customers. Anthropic agreed in August to spend $45 billion on Nscale computing capacity over six years, and Microsoft has signed a letter of intent for a campus in West Virginia, so the Essex exit does not end the relationship. But it removes an anchor tenant from a flagship project just as investors scrutinise the company’s growth story.

Execution elsewhere has also lagged. Nscale’s flagship site in Norway is reportedly running about six months behind schedule, with just over 6 MW of a planned 30 MW in operation.

The setback lands as sentiment toward so-called neoclouds, specialist providers that lease AI computing capacity and often borrow heavily to fund construction, turns more cautious. CoreWeave shares fell 25% last week, their steepest weekly drop since November, while Australian developer Firmus abandoned its planned listing after failing to draw enough investor demand at its target valuation.

The episode also highlights a growing constraint on the AI buildout: access to electricity. Demand for data centre capacity remains intense, but projects that cannot secure timely grid connections risk losing customers regardless of how much hyperscalers plan to spend.

Nscale’s IPO pricing will now be a test of whether investors view the Essex setback as an isolated power problem or as a warning about execution risk across the sector. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Only a third of the US data centre pipeline looks credible as AI financing strains build
item.description:
The repricing so far is selective rather than AI-wide: the heaviest pressure falls on companies that need outside capital to build, including Oracle, SoftBank and former bitcoin miners turned AI hosts such as Cipher and TeraWulf, while cash-rich hyperscalers like Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon are far less exposed and some of their shareholders may welcome slower capex. The second-order risk sits with Nvidia and the wider chip supply chain, where part of future demand depends on customers that have yet to secure financing. In Asia, any push-out of orders would show up first in SK Hynix, Samsung and TSMC, a meaningful risk for a chip-heavy Kospi after its strong run. At the index level, the AI build-out has been a key support for US earnings and growth, so even a slowdown rather than a collapse trims a major pillar for broader equities and, through risk sentiment, the Australian dollar. Signs that stress is spreading beyond the neoclouds, such as hyperscaler capex cuts or wider credit spreads, would mark the shift from a sector repricing to a broader market problem.

---

Info via FT, (gated) 

---

Earlier:

---

The AI boom’s binding constraint is shifting from chips to permits, power and credit, and investors are beginning to price the gap between announced data centre capacity and what can realistically be financed and built.

Summary:

  • At least 47 large US data centre projects have been delayed, withdrawn or blocked this year, a count described as conservative
  • Analysts estimate only about a third of the planned US pipeline is credible, and more than 1,000 communities have sought restrictions
  • AI infrastructure debt sold off this week, with a CoreWeave bond entering distressed territory and its shares down almost 25% on the week
  • SB Energy and Firmus have delayed or shelved listings, OpenAI has pushed back its IPO, and Nscale’s $35bn IPO target looks hard near term
  • Tenants such as Anthropic hold walk-away rights if partners miss financing or delivery deadlines
  • US AI infrastructure spending is projected to exceed $10tn between 2025 and 2032, around 3.6% of GDP a year

America’s AI infrastructure boom, projected to cost more than $10tn, is showing signs of strain as construction delays, local opposition and a sharp turn in credit markets converge on the companies racing to build data centres, the Financial Times reported.

At least 47 large US projects have been delayed, withdrawn or blocked this year, according to data from a regulatory intelligence firm that described the tally as conservative because it captures only the biggest sites. Analysts estimated this month that only about a third of the planned US data centre pipeline is credible, while more than 1,000 communities have sought moratoria or other limits on AI infrastructure in 2026.

The financing side is now under pressure too. Debt linked to AI infrastructure groups sold off sharply this week, with one CoreWeave unsecured bond sliding into distressed territory and the company’s shares losing almost a quarter of their value over the week. Bonds funding sites leased to CoreWeave also weakened, including a Virginia deal that has dropped around 5% since it priced three weeks ago. Higher interest rates and rising inflation have sharpened questions over whether revenue at leading labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic will be enough to cover the costs.

Much of the build-out depends on so-called neoclouds, young data centre providers that scaled rapidly on generous equity and debt markets, and their listing plans are stalling. SoftBank-backed SB Energy, which has yet to complete a data centre, has shelved a planned $50bn listing despite capital needs of around $175bn to fulfil roughly $430bn in contracted future revenue, mostly from OpenAI. Nscale, whose $45bn deal with Anthropic can be cancelled if it misses financing or delivery deadlines at a West Virginia project, had only 25,000 advanced chips online in August against a goal of nearly 500,000. Nebius has said it has financed only about a fifth of the roughly $250bn its planned capacity requires. OpenAI has also pushed back its own IPO.

Delays are proving expensive. Cipher agreed last month to absorb around the first $360mn of cost overruns at a Texas site in exchange for more time, a change that required roughly $750mn in extra equity, partly raised through an $850mn convertible bond this week. Several Oracle sites for OpenAI’s Stargate programme have also slipped, and Stargate lost its computing lead this week.

AI labs have chosen to risk losing part of their investment rather than face a shortage of computing power, while writing contracts that let them walk away if partners fall behind. With permits harder to win and utilities increasingly refusing grid connections to projects that cannot supply their own power, the coming months will test how much of the boom’s announced capacity actually gets built. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Putin floats Trump-Xi summit on Ukraine at APEC, leaving Kyiv out of the room
item.description:
For oil, the headline risk cuts both ways. Any credible move toward a Ukraine settlement would typically trim the risk premium tied to Russian supply, but the summit is unconfirmed and energy experts see the Iran war, not Russia, as the main driver of diesel prices, so the US diesel deal is unlikely to ease product markets much. Ukraine’s strike on a St Petersburg oil terminal and continued pressure on Russian refineries keep product supply risk alive in the near term. A softer US sanctions stance on Russia is a modest bearish factor for crude over time if it allows more Russian barrels to flow freely. For the Australian dollar, any sign of reduced great-power tension on Chinese soil would be mildly supportive for risk sentiment, though the effect is likely small until a meeting is confirmed.

---

---

Putin is trying to turn a warming relationship with Trump into a great-power deal on Ukraine without Kyiv at the table, but with no US commitment and Beijing wary of the fallout, it remains a proposal rather than a plan.

Summary:

  • Putin has proposed a three-way meeting with Trump and Xi to discuss Ukraine, reportedly on the sidelines of the November 18-19 APEC summit in Shenzhen
  • The Kremlin confirmed discussions but said there is no clear agreement on the meeting or its agenda
  • A senior US official said Trump has not agreed, though he could be receptive given his pledge to end the war
  • The idea was raised in an October 9 call that also produced a deal for the US to buy and help market Russian diesel
  • Trump paused sanctions on Russia due under a recently signed law and has stepped up criticism of Zelensky
  • China reportedly would not object if Trump joins, but Beijing worries about overshadowing APEC and straining ties with Europe

Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a three-way meeting with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month to discuss ending the war in Ukraine, a format that would exclude Kyiv and that people familiar with the talks say is designed to secure terms favourable to Moscow, the Wall Street Journal (gated) reported.

Putin raised the idea during an October 9 phone call with Trump, according to a former Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter. The same call produced an agreement for the US to buy Russian diesel and help sell it on global markets. The Kremlin has suggested holding the talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19.

What is confirmed is limited. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov acknowledged that discussions about a possible meeting are under way but said there is no clear understanding yet on whether it will happen or what it would cover. A senior US official said Trump has not agreed to a summit, although the president could be open to it given his promise to end the conflict, which is now in its fourth year. Beijing has reportedly signalled it would not object if Trump takes part.

The proposal comes as relations between Washington and Moscow have warmed noticeably. Trump paused sanctions on Russia on Friday that were due under a bipartisan law he signed last month, a move that drew criticism from lawmakers including some allies. He has also stepped up pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, demanding an end to strikes on Russian refineries after Ukraine hit an oil terminal in St Petersburg on Sunday.

The diesel deal is aimed at easing fuel prices that have weighed on the US economy ahead of the midterm elections. Energy experts, however, broadly view the Iran war as the main driver of higher diesel prices and expect the Russian volumes to have little market impact.

For Xi, hosting such talks would bolster China’s push to be seen as a global power broker, but it carries risks. Chinese officials worry a sideshow could overshadow APEC and strain economic ties with Europe, which is already wary of Beijing’s closeness to Moscow. Analysts also note that the image of three leaders negotiating over Ukraine’s future without Ukraine present could deepen concern in Taiwan.

The next markers are whether the White House formally responds and whether a meeting appears on the APEC schedule. A firm US commitment would represent a major shift in Western diplomacy on Ukraine, while a refusal would leave the existing US-led peace effort, which has largely stalled, as the only active track. 

These two easily run rings arounf you-know-who. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Oil dips as Trump waives Russia energy sanctions, offsetting Hormuz tanker blast

---

Trump has chosen to keep Russian barrels flowing to keep Moscow talking, and for now that is enough to outweigh the latest flash point in the Strait of Hormuz.

Summary:

  • Oil prices are slightly lower as futures reopen for the week
  • Trump signed an executive order waiving Graham Act sanctions and tariffs on Russian energy, drawing bipartisan criticism
  • He said on Truth Social the move aims to keep Russia in Ukraine peace talks, citing progress including on hostages, and Russia’s limited help to Iran
  • Iran’s IRGC navy said a tanker exploded after hitting a naval mine in the southern Strait of Hormuz, per Iranian media
  • Pakistan’s army chief may visit Tehran this week, ISNA reported
  • Equity and bond futures are mildly firmer; the euro lags on unrest in France and other euro area cities

Oil prices edged slightly lower as futures reopened for the week, with US President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sanctions and tariffs on Russian energy outweighing a weekend report of a tanker explosion in the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump signed an executive order waiving Graham Act sanctions and tariffs targeting Russian energy exports, a move that drew criticism from both parties in Washington. The waiver raises the prospect of more Russian fuel reaching world markets, the main reason crude traded softer in early Asian dealing.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said the decision was intended to avoid pushing Moscow away from talks on ending the war in Ukraine, saying significant progress was being made, including on hostage negotiations, and adding that signing the measure now would risk that outcome while he could do so later. He also argued that Russia was offering Iran far less help than it could, and that he wanted to keep it that way. Trump said Ukrainian strikes on Russian diesel refineries were hurting global diesel markets, including in the US, while Russia continued to ship large volumes of cheap diesel. He also sharply criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, accusing him of not wanting the war to end.

The energy angle is central for oil markets. Diesel supply has been strained by attacks on Russian refining capacity, and any easing of restrictions on Russian product exports would add barrels to a tight market at a time when the US war with Iran is already disrupting Gulf flows.

That disruption was underlined on Sunday, when Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps navy said an oil tanker caught fire and exploded after hitting a naval mine in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian media. Details of the vessel and any casualties were not immediately available, and the claim could not be independently verified.

A possible diplomatic thread also emerged, with Iran’s ISNA news agency reporting that Pakistan’s army chief, Asim Munir, may visit Tehran this week.

Elsewhere, equity and bond futures were mildly firmer, while the euro lagged amid widespread unrest in France and other major euro area cities.

For oil, the near-term balance hinges on whether the Russia waiver translates into meaningfully higher fuel exports, and whether Hormuz shipping risk escalates further.

item.title: China data preview: industry holds up, consumers and property lag ahead of Q3 GDP
item.description:
For oil, China’s position as the largest crude importer makes this release a demand signal at a sensitive moment, with the Iran war already squeezing Gulf supply. Soft domestic numbers would temper the demand side of the oil story even as supply risk keeps prices elevated. The Australian and New Zealand dollars, as proxies for Chinese growth, are exposed to any downside surprise, and the Australian dollar’s early gains against the euro could be tested. A weak print would also lift expectations for policy easing, putting Tuesday’s loan prime rate decision and the yuan in focus. An upside surprise driven mainly by exports would do little to ease concerns about trade friction.

---

More data due today:

  • Economic and event calendar in Asia - China data the focus

---

China’s export machine is running hot, but with consumers cautious, property still sinking and oil costs climbing, it is not enough to lift growth back to Beijing’s target.

Summary:

  • China’s Q3 GDP and September activity data are due at 02:00 GMT Monday (22:00 US Eastern Sunday)
  • Reuters and AFP polls both see Q3 growth at 4.4% y/y, up from 4.3% but below the 4.5% to 5.0% target; q/q growth is seen at 1.1%, from 0.9%
  • Industrial production is forecast at around 5.3% to 5.5%, retail sales at under 1%, and fixed asset investment around -7.5% year to date
  • The Iran war oil shock is adding pressure; the IMF trimmed its 2026 China forecast to 4.5%
  • Exports, driven by AI-related demand, are on course for another record surplus, fuelling trade tensions with the EU and US
  • A weak outcome would raise expectations of more stimulus, with the LPR decision due Tuesday

China’s economy is expected to have grown just short of Beijing’s official target in the third quarter, with figures due at 02:00 GMT on Monday (22:00 US Eastern on Sunday) set to show exports carrying an economy weighed down by weak domestic demand, a deep property slump and a sharp rise in energy costs.

Separate polls of economists by Reuters and AFP both point to annual growth of 4.4% for July to September, a marginal improvement on the second quarter’s 4.3% but below the government’s goal of 4.5% to 5.0% for the year, already its lowest in decades. On a quarterly basis, growth is forecast to pick up to 1.1% from 0.9%.

The September activity data, released at the same time, is expected to repeat a familiar pattern. Industrial production is forecast to accelerate slightly to around 5.3% to 5.5% from 5.2% in August, while retail sales are seen growing by less than 1%, only modestly faster than August’s 0.4%. Fixed asset investment is expected to contract further, by around 7.5% year to date, with property investment remaining the heaviest drag.

Energy has added a new layer of pressure. The US war with Iran has disrupted shipping out of the Gulf and driven up crude prices, a direct cost for the world’s largest oil importer. Citing higher oil prices and persistent structural headwinds, the International Monetary Fund last week trimmed its forecast for China’s 2026 growth to 4.5%, while describing recent support measures as limited. The IMF’s Asia and Pacific director, Krishna Srinivasan, said the shift toward consumption-led growth that economists have long urged has yet to take hold.

Exports remain the standout. Global demand for AI-related hardware, including computers, semiconductors and data centre equipment, has put China on course for another record trade surplus after last year’s $1.2 trillion. That strength is also a source of friction, with trading partners including the EU and the US increasingly critical of the surplus and of state support for Chinese industry. The EU and China agreed this month to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to Europe.

Beijing has responded with targeted support, including mortgage subsidies for some home purchases and funding for infrastructure. Goldman Sachs has warned that a second straight quarter below 4.5% would raise pressure on policymakers, and that constraints on local government finances could slow implementation. One analyst told AFP that authorities would need to deploy funds faster to meet the target.

A weaker-than-expected set of figures would strengthen the case for further stimulus in the fourth quarter, with Tuesday’s loan prime rate decision the next policy marker.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: New Zealand trade deficit widens to nearly NZ$2 billion, more than double forecasts
item.description:
A wider trade gap is a modest negative for the New Zealand dollar at the margin, since a larger external deficit means more reliance on foreign funding. Oil is the key channel to watch: with the Iran war keeping crude prices elevated, any confirmation that fuel drove the import jump would point to imported inflation pressure the RBNZ cannot ignore. That cuts against the dovish read from soft domestic demand and keeps further tightening on the table. Rate markets will weigh this against the pause they have leaned toward for 28 October. China’s growth data later today matters more for the kiwi’s near-term direction, given China’s role as a key export market.

---

New Zealand is buying more from the world while selling no more to it, and with fuel costs elevated, that imbalance lands squarely on the RBNZ’s desk ahead of a pre-election rate call.

Summary:

  • Trade balance (September): -NZ$1.971 billion vs. expected -NZ$0.775 billion (prior -NZ$1.536 billion)
  • Imports (September): NZ$8.44 billion (prior NZ$8.02 billion)
  • Exports (September): NZ$6.47 billion (prior NZ$6.48 billion)
  • The wider deficit came entirely from higher imports, with exports flat
  • The latest services index showed a fourth month of modest expansion at 50.9, with employment just below 50
  • The RBNZ, which lifted the cash rate to 2.75% in September after two straight hikes, decides next on 28 October at 01:00 GMT (21:00 US Eastern, 27 October), ahead of the 7 November election

New Zealand’s monthly trade deficit widened far more than expected in September, as imports climbed while exports stalled, adding to a run of mixed signals for the economy just over a week before the Reserve Bank of New Zealand’s next policy decision.

The goods trade shortfall came in at almost NZ$2.0 billion, more than double the roughly NZ$0.8 billion deficit economists had expected and wider than August’s gap of around NZ$1.5 billion. Imports rose to around NZ$8.4 billion from NZ$8.0 billion, while exports were essentially flat at about NZ$6.5 billion.

The detail matters as much as the headline. With exports unchanged, the entire deterioration came from the import side. A fuller breakdown by category will show how much of the rise reflects higher fuel costs, which businesses have repeatedly flagged as a concern, versus stronger demand for capital and consumer goods.

The trade figures follow the latest services survey, which showed the sector expanding for a fourth straight month in September, though only marginally, with the BNZ-BusinessNZ Performance of Services Index at 50.9. Employment in that survey sat just below the 50 line, and firms cited cost of living pressures, fuel prices, interest rates and the upcoming election as their main worries. Taken together, the two releases describe an economy that is growing, but unevenly, with households and businesses facing rising costs.

That backdrop sets up a finely balanced decision for the RBNZ on 28 October, with the announcement due at 01:00 GMT (21:00 US Eastern on 27 October). The central bank has raised the official cash rate at its last two meetings, most recently by 25 basis points to 2.75% in early September, as annual inflation climbed to 4.1% in the June quarter. Governor Anna Breman said at the time that a further increase was likely but that its timing was highly uncertain, and that policy was not on a preset course.

Market pricing has leaned toward a pause this month. The October review is a shorter statement without new forecasts, so the focus will be on whether the bank retains its tightening bias, and on any comments on the exchange rate and imported inflation.

The meeting also comes just ten days before the 7 November general election, a period that the services survey suggests is already keeping businesses cautious. A softer domestic economy argues for patience, while elevated inflation and rising import costs argue for keeping the door open to further hikes.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: New Zealand services sector grows for four months straight as PSI holds at 50.9
item.description:
A reading barely above 50 does little to shift the outlook for the New Zealand dollar, which takes its lead from global risk sentiment and rate expectations more than from second-tier surveys. A soft employment component and persistent concern over interest rates point to an economy still sensitive to borrowing costs, which supports the case for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand to stay cautious. The gap between strong manufacturing and sluggish services also suggests the recovery is not yet broad enough to drive domestic inflation. Election uncertainty is likely to keep local data in this subdued range until the result is known.

--

New Zealand’s services sector is growing again, but only just, as businesses keep their wallets shut until voters have had their say.

Summary:

  • The BNZ-BusinessNZ Performance of Services Index was 50.9 in September, from 51.0 in August and 50.5 in July
  • It’s the fourth consecutive month of expansion, following two years of contraction
  • New orders (52.6) and inventories (52.3) were the strongest components; supplier deliveries (49.4) and employment (49.8) were below 50
  • Around 60% of respondent comments were negative, little changed from August
  • Cost of living, fuel prices, interest rates and election uncertainty dominate business concerns
  • Services growth continues to lag manufacturing, which has been well above 50 for some time

New Zealand’s services sector expanded for a fourth straight month in September, though only modestly, according to the BNZ-BusinessNZ Performance of Services Index (PSI), with businesses holding back ahead of the general election.

The index registered 50.9, fractionally below August’s 51.0 but above July’s 50.5. A reading above 50 indicates expansion and below 50 contraction, so the sector remains in growth territory, but only just.

The four-month run marks a meaningful turnaround after two years in which the index sat in contraction. The pace of growth, however, remains subdued, and it continues to lag well behind manufacturing, where the equivalent Performance of Manufacturing Index has held comfortably above 50 for some time, economists noted.

Beneath the headline, the picture was uneven. New orders and inventories were the strongest components, at 52.6 and 52.3 respectively, pointing to some forward momentum in demand. Supplier deliveries were the weakest at 49.4, and employment also sat just below 50 at 49.8, a sign that firms are not yet confident enough to add staff and that the recovery remains narrowly based.

Business sentiment was little changed from August, with around 60% of respondents’ comments negative. Cost of living pressures, fuel prices, interest rates and uncertainty around the election were the dominant concerns.

BusinessNZ chief executive Katherine Rich described four consecutive months above the breakeven line as an encouraging run despite the slight easing in September. She said caution remained deeply embedded across the sector, with many businesses adopting a wait-and-see stance ahead of the election, and suggested that hesitancy was likely to cap any stronger pickup until the political outlook becomes clearer.

The result leaves the services sector on a fragile footing. With the election approaching, the coming months will show whether firms’ caution lifts once the outcome is known, or whether cost pressures and high borrowing costs continue to restrain the recovery regardless of who forms the next government.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Euro slides against Australian dollar as three European headwinds hit early trade
item.description:
The drop in EUR/AUD is a euro story first, which makes it vulnerable to a partial reversal once main Asian centres open and liquidity improves. The real test comes with the European open: French government bond spreads over Bunds and the euro’s performance against the US dollar will show whether the weekend headlines are being priced as a lasting political and fiscal risk or as a passing shock. Tuesday’s NATO council meeting is a further event risk for the euro. On the Australian side, Kent’s remarks offer the only scheduled domestic catalyst, and anything read as dovish would blunt the Aussie’s gains.

---

Earlier:

  • EUR update, France riots: 2,400 arrested as cost-of-living protests turn to looting and arson
  • US threatens EU with devastating retaliation if Brussels curbs Starlink spectrum access
  • Romanian F-16s shoot down two drones over Black Sea, NATO council to meet Tuesday

---

The Australian dollar is winning against the euro mostly by default, as Europe brings riots, drones and a trade threat to the Monday open.

Summary:

  • EUR/AUD is lower in very early Asia-Pacific trade, with flows moving out of the euro and into the Australian dollar
  • French riots over the weekend, with around 2,400 arrests, are the main weight on the euro
  • Romanian jets shooting down two drones over the Black Sea adds regional security risk, with NATO to meet on Tuesday
  • A US warning of retaliation if the EU curbs Starlink’s spectrum access adds transatlantic trade friction
  • There is little fresh Australian news, and liquidity is thin with Australian trade getting underway with earlieer trade taking place when only New Zealand was open
  • RBA Assistant Governor Christopher Kent speaks at 23:05 GMT Sunday, 19:05 US Eastern (10:05 AEDT Monday)

The euro has opened the week on the back foot against the Australian dollar, with EUR/AUD sliding in very early Asia-Pacific trade as three separate European headlines from the weekend combined to sour sentiment toward the single currency.

The biggest weight is France. A nationwide day of protest over fuel prices, wages and public services on Saturday descended into rioting, looting and arson in cities from Paris to Marseille and Limoges, with around 2,400 arrests and close to 1,000 police officers injured. President Emmanuel Macron condemned the violence but stopped short of declaring a state of emergency. For currency markets, the concern is less the damage itself than what it signals: deep social discontent in the euro area’s second-largest economy, a government with limited fiscal room to respond, and a presidential election in 2027 that the unrest has already begun to shape.

Security risk on the bloc’s eastern edge is the second factor. Romanian F-16s shot down two drones over the country’s Black Sea waters on Saturday, days after drones struck two chemical tankers off its coast. The drones’ origin has not been disclosed, and NATO allies are due to discuss the incidents at a North Atlantic Council meeting on Tuesday.

Third, transatlantic trade friction has resurfaced. The US ambassador to the EU warned European companies could face severe retaliation in the American market if Brussels presses ahead with a plan to reserve part of its satellite-to-smartphone spectrum for European operators, a move that would curb access for SpaceX’s Starlink.

There is little fresh, Australia-specific news behind the move, and it looks driven by the euro side of the cross. Early flows have favoured the Australian dollar at the euro’s expense, though with New Zealand effectively the only major centre open, liquidity is thin and early price action may exaggerate the underlying shift.

The first domestic event of note is a fireside chat with Reserve Bank of Australia Assistant Governor (Financial Markets) Christopher Kent at the Commonwealth Bank’s Global Markets Conference in Sydney, scheduled for 23:05 GMT on Sunday, 19:05 US Eastern (10:05 AEDT on Monday). Any remarks touching on the policy outlook or currency conditions would give the Australian dollar its own driver, rather than leaving it to trade purely as the beneficiary of European weakness.
